questions.q: What is the name of the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach?
questions.a: The tube is called the oesophagus. A student who says "windpipe" or "throat" confuses the digestive pathway with the respiratory system.

questions.q: Why is it important for our teeth to grind food into smaller pieces before we swallow it?
questions.a: Grinding increases the surface area of the food, allowing saliva and digestive juices to work more efficiently. A student who answers "to make it taste better" or "to make it fit in the throat" misses the scientific purpose of mechanical breakdown.

questions.q: If you were to drink a glass of water, how does the body move it down to the stomach even if you were standing on your head?
questions.a: The body uses rhythmic muscular contractions (peristalsis) to push food and liquid down the oesophagus. A student who thinks it just "falls" due to gravity ignores the muscular nature of the digestive tract.

questions.q: Compare the role of the mouth and the stomach in digestion. How are their functions different?
questions.a: The mouth performs mechanical grinding and starts sugar breakdown, while the stomach acts as a mixing chamber where food is churned with acid. A student who says they both do the same thing fails to recognize the progression of the process.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Digestion is only about making food small enough to swallow." Why is this incomplete?
questions.a: This is incomplete because digestion also involves chemical transformation into absorbable units, not just physical size reduction. A student focusing only on swallowing ignores the chemical changes required for the body to actually use the nutrients.

questions.q: Imagine a food item that is not chewed properly. Based on what you know about digestion, what might happen to the effectiveness of the stomach's work?
questions.a: The stomach will have to work much harder to break down the large chunks, which might lead to incomplete digestion or discomfort. A good answer explains that the stomach's "mixing" is less effective on large pieces than on smaller ones.
